CausalChain: Chronic liver hypoxia -> Downregulation/dysregulation of m6A reader (e.g., YTHDF2) in hepatic dendritic cells -> Reduced m6A-mediated translation of lysosomal cathepsins -> Impaired antigen degradation and cross-presentation -> Defective CD8+ T cell priming -> Establishment of an immunosuppressive microenvironment -> Promotion of HCC initiation
Hypothesis: Aberrant m6A modification in hepatic dendritic cells under hypoxic stress impairs lysosomal cathepsin translation, leading to defective antigen cross-presentation and compromised T cell priming, which facilitates immune evasion and contributes to the initiation of hepatocellular carcinoma.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains one of the most fatal cancers largely due to late detection and poor therapeutic options. Emerging evidence has implicated RNA m6A modification in the dysregulation of gene expression that underlies liver carcinogenesis. Here, we propose a novel hypothesis that links aberrant m6A modification in hepatic dendritic cells to impaired antigen processing, ultimately facilitating immune evasion and tumor initiation. Specifically, we suggest that chronic hypoxic conditions in the liver microenvironment lead to the dysregulation of m6A ‘reader’ proteins, such as YTHDF2, which in turn reduces the translation of key lysosomal cathepsins required for efficient antigen degradation and cross-presentation. This defect in antigen presentation may compromise cytotoxic T cell priming, thereby creating an immunosuppressive niche that promotes HCC development. This hypothesis provides a potential mechanistic bridge between RNA epigenetic deregulation and immune escape in liver cancer, and it may offer new targets for early diagnostic biomarkers and immunotherapeutic interventions.
